title: Transforming a continuous variable
objectives: Find the density of a transformed variable with the CDF method and with $|dx/dy|$
Use a Jacobian to transform two variables, and simulate with inverse transforms

screens.title: Uniform in, what comes out?
screens.prose: A uniform draw $U$ on $(0, 1)$ is turned into a wait $Y = -\tfrac12\ln U$. Half of all draws have $u > 0.5$. The graph shows where they land.
screens.question: What shape does the density of $Y$ have?

options.why: Half of the draws land below $y = 0.35$, a short stretch. A flat density could not pack half the draws into so little room.
The curve is steep near $u = 0$ and flat near $u = 1$. That squeezes draws together near 0 and stretches a few far to the right, not into a bell.

options.text: Piled up near 0, with a long tail to the right
Piled at large values, thinning towards 0
options.why: Large $y$ comes only from $u$ near 0, a thin slice of the draws. Most of them land at small $y$.

hints.text: Where do the draws with $u > 0.5$ end up on the $y$ axis?
They fill $y$ from 0 to 0.35. The other half is spread over everything above 0.35.

feedback.correct: Half the draws land in $[0, 0.35]$ and the rest are spread thinly out to the right.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare how much of $y$ the top half of $u$ covers with how much the bottom half covers.

byKey.flat: Half of the draws land below $y = 0.35$, a short stretch. A flat density could not do that.
byKey.bell: The curve is steep near $u = 0$ and flat near $u = 1$: draws bunch near 0 and a few stretch far right.
byKey.far: Large $y$ comes only from $u$ near 0, a thin slice of the draws.

explain.text: The upper half of $u$, which holds half the probability, maps onto $y$ in $[0, 0.35]$. The lower half is stretched over the whole rest of the axis. The density is therefore tall near 0 and thin in the tail.

screens.title: Run it and see
screens.prose: Each run draws more uniforms and transforms them. The dashed curve is an exponential density from the uniform and exponential lesson.

state.caption: Run the draws and watch the bars settle onto the dashed curve.

screens.question: The bars average about 0.5. Which rate $\lambda$ makes an exponential have mean 0.5?

hints.text: The mean of an exponential is $\tfrac{1}{\lambda}$.

feedback.correct: $\lambda = 2$: the transformed uniform is exponential with rate 2.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. The mean of an exponential is $\tfrac1\lambda$.

byKey.mean: 0.5 is the mean, not the rate. The rate is its reciprocal.

explain.text: $-\tfrac12\ln U$ has the same density as a wait with $\lambda = 2$, mean $\tfrac12$. The next screen derives that from the CDF.

screens.title: The CDF method
screens.prose: Instead of guessing, find the CDF of $Y = -\tfrac12\ln U$ and differentiate it. This is the **CDF method**.
screens.question: Put the lines in order.

lines.text: $P(Y \le y) = P\left(-\tfrac12\ln U \le y\right)$, the definition of the CDF of $Y$
$= P\left(U \ge e^{-2y}\right)$, multiplying by $-2$ flips the inequality, then exponentiating
$= 1 - e^{-2y}$, since $P(U \ge c) = 1 - c$ for a uniform $U$
$f_Y(y) = \dfrac{d}{dy}\left(1 - e^{-2y}\right) = 2e^{-2y}$, the density is the slope of the CDF

hints.text: Start from what $P(Y \le y)$ means, then rewrite the event in terms of $U$.
The slope of the CDF is the last step.

feedback.correct: Definition, rewrite in $U$, uniform chance, then differentiate.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Rewrite the event in terms of $U$ before using that $U$ is uniform.

byKey.unif: The uniform chance $1 - c$ applies once the event is written as $U \ge e^{-2y}$.
byKey.diff: Differentiating comes last, once the CDF is known.

explain.text: The CDF is $1 - e^{-2y}$, the exponential with rate 2, and its slope is $2e^{-2y}$. The dashed curve on the last screen was this density.

screens.title: Change of variables
screens.prose: You went from $U$ to $Y$ through the CDF. Let $Y = g(X)$ with $x = g^{-1}(y)$ differentiable. For strictly increasing $g$, $F_Y(y) = F_X(x)$. For strictly decreasing $g$, like $-\tfrac12\ln U$, $F_Y(y) = 1 - F_X(x)$. Either way the chain rule gives $$f_Y(y) = f_X(x)\left|\frac{dx}{dy}\right|,$$ since $\tfrac{dx}{dy} < 0$ exactly when $g$ decreases.
screens.question: For $Y = -\tfrac12\ln U$, we have $x = u = e^{-2y}$ and $f_U = 1$. What does the formula give?

options.why: You used $f_U(x)\cdot x$. The factor is the slope $\left|\tfrac{dx}{dy}\right| = 2e^{-2y}$, not $x$ itself.
You kept the sign of $\tfrac{dx}{dy}$. A density cannot be negative, so take the absolute value.
You divided by the 2 from the exponent where you should multiply. Differentiating $x = e^{-2y}$ gives $\left|\tfrac{dx}{dy}\right| = 2e^{-2y}$.

feedback.correct: $1 \times 2e^{-2y}$, the same density as the CDF method.

byKey.nofac: The factor is the slope of $x$ in $y$, not $x$.
byKey.neg: A density is never negative, so the absolute value is needed.

explain.text: $\left|\tfrac{dx}{dy}\right|$ says how much a small stretch of $y$ corresponds in $x$. Where $y$ is stretched, the density thins by exactly that factor. It reproduces the CDF method's answer.

screens.title: The lognormal density
screens.prose: A price $S = e^X$ with $X$ standard normal is lognormal. Here $x = \ln s$, so $\left|\tfrac{dx}{ds}\right| = \tfrac1s$, and $f_S(s) = f_X(\ln s)\cdot\tfrac1s$.
screens.question: What is the density $f_S(2)$?

hints.text: Find $f_X(\ln 2)$, the standard normal density at $\ln 2 = 0.6931$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Evaluate the normal density at $\ln s$, then divide by $s$.

byKey.nofac: 0.3138 is $f_X(\ln 2)$ alone. The factor $\tfrac1s$ is missing.
byKey.wayround: You multiplied by $s$ instead of dividing. The factor is $\left|\tfrac{dx}{ds}\right| = \tfrac1s$.

explain.text: $f_S(2) = \varphi(\ln 2)\cdot\tfrac12 = 0.3138 \times 0.5 = 0.1569$. The earlier lognormal density is this rule: a normal density in $\ln s$, times $\tfrac1s$.

screens.title: Inverse-transform sampling
screens.prose: Run the CDF backwards. If $U$ is uniform, $F^{-1}(U)$ has CDF $F$. For rate $\lambda$, $F(y) = 1 - e^{-\lambda y}$, so $F^{-1}(u) = -\dfrac{\ln(1 - u)}{\lambda}$.
screens.question: Write `exp_sample(rate, n, seed)`, returning `n` exponential draws.

import random


def exp_sample(rate, n, seed):

    # Use one rng.random() per draw and the inverse CDF.
    rng = random.Random(seed)
    ...
widget.solution:
import math
import random


def exp_sample(rate, n, seed):
    # n draws from an exponential with the given rate
    rng = random.Random(seed)
    return [-math.log(1 - rng.random()) / rate for _ in range(n)]

tests.call: sum(1 for y in exp_sample(2, 100000, 8) if y > 1) / 100000

hints.text: In Python, `math.log` is the natural log. Divide by `rate`.

feedback.correct: `exp_sample` matches the exact draws, and its sample mean is close to $\tfrac{1}{\text{rate}}$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Apply $F^{-1}(u) = -\ln(1 - u)/\lambda$ to each uniform draw.

explain.text: Each draw is one uniform pushed through $F^{-1}$. At 100,000 draws the standard error of the sample mean is about 0.3% of $\tfrac{1}{\text{rate}}$, so the mean lands within a percent of it. Any CDF you can invert gives a sampler this way.

screens.title: Two branches
screens.prose: Let $Z$ be standard normal and $Y = Z^2$. Both $z = \sqrt y$ and $z = -\sqrt y$ give the same $y$, so add the two branches, each with its own factor $\left|\tfrac{dz}{dy}\right| = \tfrac{1}{2\sqrt y}$.
screens.question: What is $f_Y(1)$?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Add the contribution of $z = 1$ and of $z = -1$.

byKey.one: 0.1210 is one branch. The value $y = 1$ comes from both $z = 1$ and $z = -1$.
byKey.nofac: 0.4839 adds the two branches but leaves out the factor $\tfrac{1}{2\sqrt y}$ on each.

explain.text: $f_Y(y) = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi y}}e^{-y/2}$, so $f_Y(1) = 0.2420$. This is the **chi-square** density with one degree of freedom. It blows up at $y = 0$ yet its area is 1, as in the improper-integral lesson.

screens.title: Forgetting the stretch
screens.prose: $X$ is uniform on $[0, 1]$ with $f_X = 1$, and $Y = 3X$ runs over $[0, 3]$. A learner writes $f_Y(y) = f_X(y/3) = 1$ on $[0, 3]$ and checks the area on the graph.
screens.question: Which is the density of $Y$?

options.why: You substituted $x = y/3$ and stopped. The area under it is 3, so it is not a density.
You multiplied by $\tfrac{dy}{dx} = 3$ instead of $\left|\tfrac{dx}{dy}\right| = \tfrac13$. The area would be 9.
The height is right but $Y$ reaches 3, not 1. That area is only $\tfrac13$.

hints.text: A density must have area 1. What is the area under height 1 over $[0, 3]$?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check that the area under your candidate is 1.

byKey.one: You substituted $x = y/3$ and stopped. The area is 3.
byKey.three: You multiplied by $\tfrac{dy}{dx}$. The factor is $\left|\tfrac{dx}{dy}\right|$.
byKey.short: The height is right but $Y$ reaches 3.

explain.text: Stretching by 3 spreads the same probability over three times the width, so the height drops to $\tfrac13$. Always check the area: a candidate that does not integrate to 1 has lost its $\left|\tfrac{dx}{dy}\right|$.

screens.title: Box and Muller
screens.prose: Two independent uniforms $U_1, U_2$ give $R = \sqrt{-2\ln U_1}$ and $\Theta = 2\pi U_2$. In two dimensions the factor is the Jacobian determinant. Find the density of $(R, \Theta)$, then of $X = R\cos\Theta$, $Y = R\sin\Theta$.
screens.question: Put the lines in order.

lines.text: $u_1 = e^{-r^2/2}$ and $u_2 = \tfrac{\theta}{2\pi}$, solving the map for the uniforms
$\left|\dfrac{\partial(u_1, u_2)}{\partial(r, \theta)}\right| = \left|-re^{-r^2/2}\right|\cdot\dfrac{1}{2\pi}$, a triangular determinant: $u_1$ depends on $r$ only and $u_2$ on $\theta$ only
$f(r, \theta) = 1 \cdot \dfrac{re^{-r^2/2}}{2\pi}$, the uniform density 1 times the Jacobian
$= \dfrac{e^{-x^2/2}}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\cdot\dfrac{e^{-y^2/2}}{\sqrt{2\pi}}$, using $r^2 = x^2 + y^2$: two independent standard normals

hints.text: Express the old variables in terms of the new ones first.
The Jacobian multiplies the old density 1. Polar area then brings in a factor $r$.
Invert, Jacobian, density in $(r, \theta)$, divide by $r$, factor.

feedback.correct: Invert, take the Jacobian, convert the area element, then factor.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. You need the uniforms in terms of $r, \theta$ before the determinant.

byKey.jac: The Jacobian needs $u_1$ and $u_2$ written in terms of $r$ and $\theta$ first.
byKey.xy: The division by $r$ comes after the density in $(r, \theta)$ is known.
byKey.fac: Factoring is the last step, once $f(x, y)$ is written in $r^2 = x^2 + y^2$.

explain.text: The density factors into two standard normal densities, so $X$ and $Y$ are independent $N(0, 1)$. Every simulator that needs normals can start from two uniforms this way.

screens.title: Normals from uniforms
screens.prose: Turn the derivation into a sampler. Each pair of uniforms gives two normals, $R\cos\Theta$ and then $R\sin\Theta$.
screens.question: Write `box_muller(n, seed)`, returning a list of $2n$ standard normal draws.

widget.starter:
import math
import random


def box_muller(n, seed):
    # a list of 2n standard normal draws, cosine then sine for each pair
    rng = random.Random(seed)
    out = []
    for _ in range(n):
        u1 = 1 - rng.random()  # in (0, 1], so the log is safe
        u2 = rng.random()
        ...
    return out
widget.solution:
import math
import random


def box_muller(n, seed):
    # a list of 2n standard normal draws
    rng = random.Random(seed)
    out = []
    for _ in range(n):
        u1 = 1 - rng.random()
        u2 = rng.random()
        r = math.sqrt(-2 * math.log(u1))
        theta = 2 * math.pi * u2
        out.append(r * math.cos(theta))
        out.append(r * math.sin(theta))
    return out

screens.title: A lump of probability
screens.prose: A call with strike £105 pays $\max(S - 105, 0)$. The price at expiry is $N(100, 10^2)$. The map $g(s) = \max(s - 105, 0)$ is constant for every $s \le 105$.
screens.question: What is $P(\text{payoff} = 0)$?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. The payoff is 0 whenever $S \le 105$.

byKey.tail: 0.3085 is the chance the call finishes in the money. The question asks about a payoff of 0.
byKey.zero: A single value of $S$ has chance 0, but the payoff piles every $S \le 105$ onto the value 0.

explain.text: A strictly increasing or strictly decreasing $g$ with $g' \ne 0$ keeps a density. A $g$ that is constant on an interval collapses that interval's probability onto a single value, here 0.6915 at 0. The payoff has an **atom** at 0 and a density above it.

screens.title: Simulating a loan book
screens.prose: A Monte Carlo engine simulates a book of 100 names, each with default hazard 2% a year. For each name it draws a uniform $U$ and sets $T = -\dfrac{\ln(1 - U)}{0.02}$ years.
screens.question: How many of the 100 names should default within 5 years, on average?

hints.text: A name defaults within 5 years when $T \le 5$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Use $P(T \le 5) = 1 - e^{-0.1}$ and multiply by 100.

byKey.linear: 10 is rate times time times names. For a chance, use $1 - e^{-\lambda t}$, which is a little smaller.
byKey.prob: 0.0952 is the chance for one name. Multiply by 100 names.

explain.text: The draw triggers a default when $U < 1 - e^{-0.1} = 0.0952$, so about 9.5 of 100 names default. Monte Carlo engines start from uniforms, and $F^{-1}(U)$ turns them into any distribution whose CDF can be inverted.

ideas: The CDF method finds $P(Y \le y)$ and differentiates. For strictly monotone $g$ with a differentiable inverse it gives $f_Y(y) = f_X(x)\left|\tfrac{dx}{dy}\right|$.
A map that is not one-to-one (like $Z^2$) needs one term per branch. A map constant on an interval leaves an atom.
In two dimensions the factor is the Jacobian determinant. Box and Muller turn two uniforms into two independent normals.

formula.name: Change of variables
formula.tex: f_Y(y) = f_X(x)\left|\dfrac{dx}{dy}\right|, \qquad f_{V,W} = f_{X,Y}\left|\dfrac{\partial(x, y)}{\partial(v, w)}\right|
formula.note: Check that the new density has area 1. If it does not, a factor is missing.

summary.trap: Leaving out $\left|\tfrac{dx}{dy}\right|$ gives a curve that does not integrate to 1. Taking one branch of $Z^2$ halves the density.

quiz.question: What is the height of the density of $Y$?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. $Y$ is spread over $[0, 2]$ and the area must stay 1.

explain.text: $\left|\tfrac{dx}{dy}\right| = \tfrac12$, so the height is $\tfrac12$. Width 2 times height $\tfrac12$ is 1.

quiz.question: What wait does the uniform draw $u = 0.9$ give?

byKey.half: 0.3413 is only the branch $0 \le Z \le 1$. $Z$ may also be between $-1$ and 0.
byKey.upper: 0.8413 is $P(Z \le 1)$. That includes every negative $Z$, even those with $Z^2 > 1$.

quiz.prose: In Box and Muller, $R^2 = -2\ln U_1$ and $X^2 + Y^2 = R^2$ for two independent standard normals.
quiz.question: What is $E[R^2]$?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. $R^2$ is the sum of two squared standard normals.

byKey.one: 1 is the mean of one squared normal. $R^2$ adds two of them.
byKey.four: 4 would need each squared normal to have mean 2. Each has mean 1.

explain.text: Each standard normal has $E[Z^2] = 1$, so $E[R^2] = 2$. Check from the uniform: $-\ln U_1$ has mean 1, so $-2\ln U_1$ has mean 2.
